proof_attempt_summary: The proposed universal quadratic full-model information boundary was refuted by rare-region observed-DQM counterexamples. Discovery retained the analytic quadratic calculation, transfer conditions, a positive-residual-variance exact boundary, and attainment on ordinary and specified continuous rescue subclasses. Independent raw-I/O validity review confirmed the actual math-referee pass, but the unrestricted boundary and adaptive unknown-geometry attainment remain open; no Lean formalization was entered.
tldr: A coarse randomized trial supplies finitely many averages of a shared treatment-effect function; an independent registry estimates their within-cell covariate composition. The analytic information cost is an explicit quadratic with separate coarse-trial and registry penalties. Law-adaptive regular transfer identifies the full observed tangent closure. Ordinary square-integrability of a feasible whole residual weight suffices for full-model efficiency, and a positive residual-variance lower bound makes the analytic range condition the exact finite-information boundary. This covers strict precision gains and a continuous infinite-to-finite rescue without bounded covariate density ratios. Cross-fitting attains the bound with uniform Wald coverage on the two declared subclasses. Two rare-region witnesses separate finite analytic cost from full regularity and analytic from full tangent closure. A third explicit borderline-density witness proves that the proposed regular residual condition is sufficient rather than necessary.
gap: Common-covariate efficiency, general fusion geometry, and finite-dimensional aggregate-effect estimation do not by themselves solve the unrestricted coarsened-trial information problem with independently estimated conditional composition.
fill: The kernel is the explicit \(J(\alpha)\) frontier and legal tangent-closure theorem. Its empirical counterpart estimates finite coarse coefficients and the residual weight jointly, preserving the registry variance and both target and registry empirical processes.
